quick: Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy: 1 g (3 MIU) orally every 8 hours (3 g/day). General: 6-9 MIU/day
Take on an empty stomach; food may reduce absorption
Drug of choice for acute maternal toxoplasmosis to reduce vertical transmission; concentrates in placenta
Excreted in breast milk; use with caution
No major adjustment usually needed (minimal renal excretion)
Caution - hepatic metabolism/biliary excretion; rare hepatotoxicity
GI tolerance; rare hepatic and allergic reactions; QT in predisposed
summary: Spiramycin is a macrolide antibiotic used mainly to treat acute Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy to reduce the risk of transmission to the fetus, and for various respiratory, oropharyngeal, and soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible organisms. It concentrates in the placenta. NOTE: spiramycin is NOT FDA-approved in the United States (available via the FDA for toxoplasmosis on a case basis); it is licensed and widely used in Europe and elsewhere (EMA/SmPC, BNF).
indications: Acute toxoplasmosis in pregnancy (to reduce maternal-fetal transmission before fetal infection is confirmed)
Respiratory tract infections caused by susceptible organisms
Skin and soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible bacteria

dosage.d: 1 g (3 million IU) orally every 8 hours
dosage.n: Continue until delivery or until fetal infection confirmed (then switch to pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine)

dosage.d: 6-9 million IU (2-3 g) per day in 2-3 divided doses
dosage.n: Severe infection up to higher divided doses per SmPC

admin: Administer orally, preferably on an empty stomach
For toxoplasmosis in pregnancy, continue therapy as directed until delivery or until amniocentesis/PCR clarifies fetal status
Complete the prescribed course for bacterial infections
If fetal infection is confirmed, treatment is generally switched to pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine (with folinic acid)
moa: A macrolide that binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible organisms, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic). Against Toxoplasma gondii it concentrates in placental tissue, reducing parasite transmission across the placenta; it does not reliably cross to treat established fetal infection.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to spiramycin or other macrolides
relative: Congenital or acquired QT prolongation / concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
monitor: Signs of hypersensitivity or skin reactions
ECG/QT in patients with risk factors

preg: Spiramycin is the recommended first-line agent for acute maternal toxoplasmosis acquired in pregnancy because it concentrates in the placenta and reduces vertical transmission, and it is not teratogenic. It does not adequately treat established fetal infection, for which pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is used after the first trimester.
lact: Spiramycin is excreted in breast milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding; monitor the infant for GI upset.
renal: Renal excretion is minor; no significant dose adjustment is generally required in renal impairment.
hepatic: Metabolized in the liver and excreted largely in bile; use with caution in hepatic impairment as rare hepatotoxicity (cholestasis, hepatitis) can occur.

major: QT-prolonging drugs / Class IA and III antiarrhythmics (additive risk of torsades, especially IV use)
moderate: Levodopa/carbidopa (spiramycin reduces carbidopa absorption - reduced levodopa levels)
minor: Unlike erythromycin/clarithromycin, spiramycin has minimal CYP3A4 inhibition - fewer drug interactions
interactions.food: Food may reduce absorption - take on an empty stomach

serious: QT prolongation (mainly with IV use or risk factors)
rare: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis and other severe cutaneous reactions

monitoring: Signs of hypersensitivity or skin reaction
Liver function if therapy is prolonged or symptoms arise
ECG/QT in patients with cardiac risk factors or on IV therapy
counsel: Take on an empty stomach and complete the full course
In pregnancy, this medicine helps protect your baby from the toxoplasmosis infection - keep taking it as directed
Report rash, itching, severe diarrhea, or yellowing of skin/eyes
Tell your doctor about heart rhythm problems or other medicines you take
pk: Antibacterial activity within hours of absorption; tissue accumulation over days
Plasma peak ~1.5-3 hours after an oral dose
Concentrates and persists in tissues (and placenta) longer than in plasma, supporting 2-3 times daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from moisture and light
pearls: NOT FDA-approved in the US - obtained for toxoplasmosis in pregnancy through the FDA on a case-by-case basis; licensed via EMA/SmPC and listed in the BNF
First-line for acute maternal toxoplasmosis to prevent transplacental transmission; concentrates in placenta but does not treat established fetal infection
Switch to pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (with folinic acid) if fetal infection is confirmed (after first trimester)
Few CYP3A4 interactions compared with erythromycin/clarithromycin
Notable interaction: reduces absorption of carbidopa, lowering levodopa effect
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular schedule - do not double up.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Overdose may cause gastrointestinal symptoms; QT prolongation has been reported, particularly in neonates and with IV use. Management is supportive with ECG monitoring and correction of any QT prolongation or electrolyte disturbance.
